canberra.title: The Canberra Bookshelf: Intrigue, revenge, family secrets and the importance of point of view
canberra.snippet: To some extent Full Circle is a departure for Chris Hammer (Summit Books, an imprint of Simon and Schuster, Australia, 2026; cover Luke C...
canberra.content:
The stock market is the weapon of choice for two wealthy families vying for top dog status in this tale of murder and greed.

To some extent Full Circle is a departure for Chris Hammer (Summit Books, an imprint of Simon and Schuster, Australia, 2026; cover Luke Causby/Blue Cork; cover image ID 31944674 Rad100/Dreamtime.com).

Set in the rarefied air of the uber wealthy in Sorrento, Victoria, and the heady world of high finance and its potential for white-collar crime, the story centres on dynasties, revenge and deadly secrets. Two wealthy families vie for top dog status, and the stock market is the weapon of choice, while violent murders are also seemingly de rigueur.

Hero of the tale is Travis Somerland, erstwhile undercover cop, wracked with self-loathing and guilt following the death of his lover. He goes to work as a driver for filthy rich Felix Clapton on his property Montechino and is soon embroiled in a power struggle to bring down rival family the Murtries – the very family who has murdered his girlfriend and ruined his life.

We jump back 16 months for a second point of view by Judy Bleuski, a backstory that fills in some holes in our understanding but equally creates more puzzles.

It is soon obvious that money is the means to many ends, including bringing down one’s rivals – the having of it, the losing of it, the making and annihilation of fortunes through financial trading sleight of hand and skulduggery, though nothing strictly illegal, but that mercilessly sweeps the little people up in its wake.

With characteristic command of his metier, Chris Hammer takes us back and forth in time and cunningly braids together the various plots, subplots and backstories to a conclusion that still leaves questions hanging in the air. His fascinating cast of characters demands our constant attention, horrified though it is for the most part.

What is clear in this work is that money delivers power and together they corrupt even the most apparently incorruptible. The casual wearing of wealth and the assumption of entitlement it lends are ugly and ruthless.

As usual, held by Hammer’s supreme craftsmanship, we cannot look away.

An insightful psychological study of human behaviour and the complexities of family.

In She Lied First (HarperCollinsPublishers, Australia 2026; cover Maya Abraham; cover images Jimena Roquero/stocksy.com /5852005; ohlamourstudio/stocksy.com/4516591; shutterstock.com), point of view is not merely the dominant storytelling technique – it is indeed a large part of what the book is about.

Dinuka McKenzie has deftly controlled her readers’ understanding of events in this thrilling psychological work by carefully filtering what we learn from the first to the last page.

Sisters Devika and Kalyani are in a constant dance of truth and lies. Devika is determined to escape the controls and expectations of her mother Rupa. Kalyani is desperately seeking connection and love, a sense of belonging.

Their lives become entwined in a most troubling way as they grapple with the moral question of what truths we should tell those we love the most. It is in both their interests to keep secrets, but therein lies the path to the fatal outcome of this tale.

Another perspective is provided via Nate, the main male actor in the book. Devika’s efforts to reveal what she believes to be his toxic behaviour are a major distraction for the reader – again our view fluctuates the more we realise how narrowly we are allowed to see Nate at first. As with the other characters, he does not necessarily cover himself with glory, but is eventually somewhat redeemed.

Rupa is another interesting one. Because so much of what we believe about her comes from Devika, it is only as we learn her history from her own point of view that we once again realise how skewed our view of her has been.

Sri Lankan cultural issues inform so much of Rupa’s behaviour, and the generational conflict between mother and daughter creates ongoing tension. In part, this provides the opportunity for subtle commentary on racism and Australian society in general.

This book is an insightful psychological study of human behaviour. It is also a study of the complexities of family, matters of the heart (and body) and the constraints placed on us all by obligation and, indeed, love.

It’s a very clever mix of tightly controlled obfuscation and ripping yarn – engrossing fiction, unsettling until the last climactic revelation.

canberra.title: After a decade of abuse, Canberra mum pushes for ‘right to know’ a partner’s violent past
canberra.snippet: For almost 10 years, Canberra mother Emma Poppe struggled to recognise the full extent of the domestic violence she was experiencing. She...
canberra.content:
Canberra mother Emma Poppe is calling for a domestic violence disclosure scheme that would allow people to seek information about a partner’s history of violence. Photo: Supplied

For almost 10 years, Canberra mother Emma Poppe struggled to recognise the full extent of the domestic violence she was experiencing. She tried to leave repeatedly, lost contact with family and friends, and suffered in silence while those around her had little idea what was happening behind closed doors.

Now, looking back, one question continues to trouble her: Would things have been different if she had known more about the warning signs of abuse, or had access to information about a partner’s history of violence?

It is a question she cannot answer with certainty, but one that has prompted her to launch a petition calling for the ACT to introduce a domestic and family violence disclosure scheme, commonly known as Clare’s Law.

The proposal would allow people concerned about a current or former partner to request information from police about any relevant history of domestic violence, including convictions, protection orders and breaches.

For Ms Poppe, a mother of three young children, the campaign is both deeply personal and about preventing others from experiencing similar harm.

“Over the past 12 months, I have spent a considerable amount of time reflecting on what I experienced throughout almost a decade of my life,” she told Region.

“Would I have recognised certain behaviours sooner? Would I have understood the warning signs? Would having access to information about a person’s history of violence have helped me make different decisions?”

She said her experience was not something people around her could easily see.

“I became disconnected from my family, stopped contacting friends, and people I worked alongside had absolutely no idea what I was experiencing behind closed doors.

“There were periods when I would go days without eating, spend my nights crying myself to sleep, and constantly wonder how I was ever going to find a way out of the circumstances I was living in.”

She said it took nearly a decade to fully understand what she had been experiencing, and she attempted to leave more times than she could count.

“Sometimes it is not until you are deeply entrenched in an abusive relationship that you begin to recognise the seriousness of what is happening around you.”

The petition asks the Legislative Assembly to call on the ACT Government to investigate, develop and implement a disclosure scheme after consultation with victim-survivors, domestic violence services, police and legal experts.

Under the proposed system, people could confidentially ask police to assess whether their partner has a relevant history of domestic violence.

It would also allow family members, friends or professionals to raise concerns about someone they believe may be at risk.

A separate provision would let police consider proactively warning a person when information indicates they may face serious danger.

The petition proposes examining whether disclosures could include past family violence orders, convictions, breaches, police reports and, with appropriate safeguards, pending charges. It also calls for access to relevant interstate information.

However, Ms Poppe acknowledges that access to information alone will not prevent domestic violence.

“I cannot say with certainty that a disclosure scheme would have changed my personal circumstances, or what information might have been available to me had such a scheme existed,” she said.

“But I do believe that earlier access to relevant information, accompanied by education and specialist support, has the potential to help someone recognise patterns of abusive behaviour before their circumstances escalate.”

She is particularly concerned that discussions about domestic violence too often focus on why victims stay rather than the barriers preventing them from leaving.

“I also want to emphasise that leaving an abusive relationship is rarely as simple as making the decision to walk away.

“There can be enormous emotional, psychological, financial and safety barriers involved. For many victim-survivors, leaving can itself be an incredibly frightening and dangerous time.”

Her petition therefore calls for professional risk assessments, confidential processes, safety planning and specialist support to accompany any disclosure.

It also seeks safeguards to protect privacy, procedural fairness and the confidentiality of victim-survivors.

The proposed scheme would not be a public register of alleged offenders, but a structured process for assessing and sharing relevant information where safety concerns arise.

Ms Poppe said the need for better support became painfully clear during her own attempts to seek help.

She stressed that her experience was not a criticism of frontline workers, whom she deeply respected, but raised questions about whether services had enough resources to meet demand.

“We need to ensure that when somebody finally finds the courage to reach out for help, that help is accessible.”

Beyond the disclosure scheme, Ms Poppe wants greater education about coercive control, financial abuse, emotional manipulation and other behaviours that may not initially be recognised as domestic violence.

She believes this education should begin early, before young people enter relationships.

As a mother, she said her children were a major motivation for speaking publicly about her experience. “I want my children to grow up understanding that love should never involve fear, intimidation, control or abuse.”

“We cannot expect our children to recognise behaviours that we have never taught them to identify.”

She hopes the ACT will examine disclosure schemes operating in other jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom and parts of Canada, and learn from their successes and limitations before developing a local model. The petition also calls for ongoing independent evaluation and a nationally consistent approach, so access to relevant safety information does not depend on where someone lives.

Ms Poppe said the petition had attracted nearly 200 signatures within a day of opening. It currently has more than 300 signatories.

While encouraged by the response, she is realistic about what a single reform could achieve. “This scheme alone will not fix domestic and family violence, but I believe it represents a meaningful step in the right direction.”

For her, the petition marks the start of a broader effort to improve prevention, education and support, especially for the next generation.

“I don’t want my experiences to simply become part of another domestic violence statistic. I want them to become part of the reason we start doing things differently.”

The petition to Establish an ACT Domestic and Family Violence Disclosure Scheme is supported by independent MLA Leanne Castley. It opened on 6 October and will remain open until 6 April 2027.

canberra.title: Unique African Restaurant shares untold stories through great food
canberra.snippet: African food has historically been underrepresented in Canberra’s hospitality scene, but a new restaurant is setting out to change ...
canberra.content:
Sylverline Uzomanze and Promise Okwuchukwu offer warm hospitality at Unique African Restaurant. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

African food has historically been underrepresented in Canberra’s hospitality scene, but a new restaurant is setting out to change that.

Although Sylverline Uzomanze and Promise Okwuchukwu both honed their cooking skills in their home country of Nigeria, the two actually met in Canberra. They cooked together twice at the National Multicultural Festival and Africa in the Park events before deciding they wanted to open a restaurant together.

“We wanted people to have easy access to African food, because people love it,” Promise told Region.

Sylverline said they wanted to use their restaurant as an opportunity to tell stories.

“Africa is an amazing place, we have amazing people and we have amazing food. Where we come from in Nigeria, food is what brings people together,” she said.

“There are so many untold stories about Africa, and there’s no better way to share those stories than through a meal. We’re trying to create a space where people can come and dine in and learn about Africa.”

You must try the jollof rice. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

The result is the newly opened Unique African Restaurant in Civic’s West Row. The large space includes a dining room with black tablecloths, gilded chairs and stunning portraits hung on the walls and a space for private functions. Sylverline said they’re hoping to host birthday parties or corporate events there.

The restaurant is open for lunch and dinner, but the team is also planning to expand to include breakfast. The a la carte menu offers a diverse selection of West African classics like jollof rice (cooked with tomato, capsicum spices) and pepper soup; a spicy stew of meat or fish in an aromatic broth.

Promise recommends a grilled dish like suya as a dish for newcomers to try.

“Suya is grilled beef skewers served with peanuts and spices, which give it that very bold African taste. And our grilled platters with side dishes like yam are good to share.”

Sharing among friends is a great way to experience a range of dishes, but there are also solo-sized plates available for lunch.

If you’d prefer to try a little bit of everything all at once, Unique African Restaurant also has you covered.

“We are planning to do a buffet once or twice every month so people can have a taste of a variety of meals, and they can come back and pick their favourite to order next time,” Sylverline said.

Puff puff doughnuts are a delicious treat. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Unique African Restaurant. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Fried Rice with Chicken. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Egusi Soup. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Unique African Restaurant. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

When I visited for lunch, Promise gave me a range of dishes to try.

First up: puff-puff. These hand-shaped doughnuts can be eaten as sweet or savoury bites. I opted to have them with a pepper sauce and I’m glad I did. The accompanying relish of silky capsicum was sweet and spicy and absolutely delicious.

Promise’s jollof rice was a little spicier and smokier than I’ve tried elsewhere, and was pure comfort with a side of chicken and plantain. I also had a taste of egusi soup, made with melon seeds, greens, dried crayfish and goat meat. Eaten with pinches of fufu (mashed yam), the strong crayfish flavours were tempered and balanced. The greens added a freshness and, despite being very full, I had a few more mouthfuls.

While both Sylverline and Promise are Nigerian, the menu is intentionally not just Nigerian food, rather a celebration of African food in general. They’re planning to have nights that focus on individual countries; sharing unique meals, celebrating culture and inviting guest chefs.

After a grand opening in early September, Sylverline said the feedback from customers had been really encouraging. One guest said the food made him feel like he was back home in his country, others were excited to try something completely new.

But no matter whether their guests are African diaspora looking for a taste of home or other Canberrans looking for something different, for Sylverline and Promise it’s all about hospitality, culture, and good food.

“Putting in the effort and seeing people appreciate what you do, it feels really good.”

Unique African Restaurant is located at 43/24 West Row, Canberra City. It is open from 11 am to 9 pm, Tuesday to Sunday, with breakfast hours coming soon.
Follow Unique African Restaurant on Facebook or Instagram.

canberra.title: Couture, activewear, wearable art: Breadth of First Nations fashion on show in landmark event
canberra.snippet: The National Museum of Australia will come alive in a celebration of First Nations fashion, culture and story-telling in a landmark event...
canberra.content:
Canberra-born Jahna Lugnan has walked catwalks from Darwin to New York. She says the nation’s capital misses out when it comes to First Nation fashion. Photo: Jess Whaler, Yuluwirri Studios

The National Museum of Australia will come alive in a celebration of First Nations fashion, culture and story-telling in a landmark event showcasing local and national Indigenous designers, models, artists and performers.

On Saturday 17 October, Kultural Dreaming Capital Runway will bring together more than 30 models and 13 designers to showcase everything from casual and activewear to wearable art and couture.

Organisers say it’s the first event of its kind for the nation’s capital – but it won’t be the last.

The event is co-produced by Kathleen Bolt and Jahna Lugnan of Indigenous Kultural Creations and Kristie Peters of Blaklabel Dreaming.

“We’re putting it on the map,” Ms Bolt said.

“We want everyone to walk away with a wow factor and say, ‘Oh my God, when is the next one?’.”

A Nyangbal-Githabal-Bandjalang-Widjabal woman, Ms Bolt is also a former Independent candidate for Murrumbidgee and one half of the mother-daughter dream team behind Indigenous Kultural Creations.

Though her daughter Jahna simply calls her “Momager”.

At 20, Jahna, a Bundjalung/Gumbaynaggirr woman, is an emerging yet already seasoned model, performer and fashion industry leader.

She has walked the runways at New York Fashion Week and Australian Fashion Week as a brand ambassador for First Nations fashion label Buluuy Mirrii and showcased countless other First Nations designers on catwalks from Darwin to the Gold Coast.

Jahna, who was born in Canberra, said the nation’s capital typically missed out when it came to First Nation fashion.

“We always have to travel to do things. There’s just never any opportunities here, so this is going to open a lot of doors.”

Kultural Dreaming Capital Runway aims to shine much-needed light on Ngunnawal-country based designers such as Yarrudhmarra Dreaming & Blaklabel Dreaming, Corella & Crow, Harry’s Clarry, DDesigns and Pakana Dreaming.

“They just do not get enough recognition,” she said.

“We’re hoping to offer that exposure and that there will be key people in the audience to offer new opportunities.”

As well as unlocking opportunities, Ms Bolt and Jahna want to create an environment in which First Nations talent is properly supported and respected – from cultural authenticity to respecting modesty.

“I think it’s one of the biggest problems in the industry,” Jahna said.

“There’s cultural protocols that don’t always align with what others are doing.”

The duo has been supporting models and designers since 2021, when the pair held its first runway event on the Gold Coast.

Through their business, Indigenous Kultural Creations, they support models with their personal growth, confidence, cultural identity and leadership.

They do whatever they can to help community members reach their goals.

“If someone from the community comes to us and says ‘I’d like to model at Australian Fashion Week’, we work towards a goal of getting them there. And if they get accepted, then we support that through finding funding for accommodation and travel,” Jahna said.

“Even if I have to drive them myself.”

Ms Bolt, pictured modelling Pakana Dreaming, says Kultural Dreaming Capital Runway aims to shine much-needed light on Ngunnawal-country based designers. Photo: Jess Whaler, Yuluwirri Studios.

The benefits of their approach extend beyond the runway and into the community.

“We work with community and those who’ve have a disadvantaged backgrounds … or are struggling in life,” Jahna said.

“We introduce them to modelling and build them up to become positive.”

Workshops combine modelling skills such as deportment, grooming and personal presentation with mentoring, leadership and self-care. They also encourage conversations around difficult issues like mental health and suicide awareness.

“Whatever they do, we won’t leave them at the altar. We’ll walk them through their life. We’ll always be there.

“Our community can be disconnected at times, so it’s also bringing mobs back together to celebrate the spirits of someone else’s storyline, history and achievements.”

It’s that spirit of celebration that Ms Bolt says audiences can expect to see brought to life at the Kultural Dreaming Capital Runway – with a few surprises along the way.

“We have a surprise performer singing to one of the designers,” she teases.

“I can’t tell you about that … but it’s going to be amazing.”

Kultural Dreaming Capital Runway takes place on Saturday 17 October at the National Museum of Australia. Click here for tickets.

canberra.title: Return of pool noodles to stop cygnets being swept away ‘tricky’ decision, says rescue group
canberra.snippet: While a pool noodle barrier would help keep cygnets on Queanbeyan River safe, it’s unclear whether one will be reinstalled this yea...
canberra.content:
10 October 2026

Start the conversation

A pool noodle barrier has kept previous generations of cygnets safe, but will it make a return? Photo: Supplied.

While a pool noodle barrier would help keep cygnets on Queanbeyan River safe, it’s unclear whether one will be reinstalled this year.

In 2021, Wildcare Queanbeyan installed a pool noodle barrier that kept a previous brood of cygnets from being swept over the Queanbeyan River weir.

With the recent arrival of new babies, bird coordinator Maryanne Gates said the group was monitoring whether they’ll need to put the barrier back in place.

“It worked a treat,” she said.

“The pool noodles are still in our storage area and ready to go if it’s required.”

She said that while some people had called for its return, it would be a “tricky” process and some in the community were concerned about the noodles contaminating the water.

“Some people have asked why we don’t just put it up,” she said.

“I wish it was that easy. We have to get the cooperation of Queanbeyan Council and the SES to help us.”

She and a fellow Wildcare volunteer had a “brainwave” after seeing cygnets tumble over the weir.

“When we invented the pool noodle barrier – which is the first time I believe it has been used anywhere – the two of us went to Bunnings.

“We bought lots and lots of pool noodles. The staff at the time asked if we were having a pool party because of the quantity that we bought!”

Using stainless steel wire to string the noodles together, the rescue group had a flexible barrier.

After getting approvals from Queanbeyan-Palernag Regional Council (QPRC), they partnered with the SES unit to install it using one of their boats.

While Mr and Ms Swan won hearts as treasured community members, Ms Gates believes the pair currently raising cygnets are newcomers.

“They seemed to be quite savvy with raising their babies,” she said of the former couple.

“We hope the current parents know to keep the little ones away from there.”

Their barrier first went up in 2021, but ultimately had to be replaced when a storm blew it away. It was later removed and put into storage when other swan parents kept their cygnets away from the weir.

“We’re waiting to see whether they are in danger of going over the edge,” she said of the new cygnets.

Ms Gates said the swan families who had made their homes in the Queanbeyan River were mostly in good health, but predators and fishing line meant they could fall into strife.

“We’ve never had a problem with the health of the family, except for when fishing line or dogs have been involved.

“There are a few things that cause the cygnets to disappear – there are occasionally dogs off lead [that] have attacked the cygnets, as has happened in other places. Our native rakali will take a cygnet.”

Ms Gates urges anyone who finds a swan that looks to be in trouble to call Wildcare.

“We rely heavily on members of the public to keep us informed,” she said.

“I know some people worry that it’s too late once they go over the weir … They don’t die from going over the weir.

“They just can’t get back to their parents – and they need their parents for safety, because they’re more vulnerable [at that age].”

If a cygnet does go over the weir, you can call Wildcare Queanbeyan’s 24-hour hotline on (02) 6299 1966.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

australia.title: Australia does not ‘need or want Russian fuel’, Chris Bowen says, after Trump deal to buy diesel from Putin
australia.snippet: Energy and climate change minister says Russia should not be rewarded for ‘illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine’ Get our breaking news...
australia.content:
Australia’s energy minister has said Russia “should not be rewarded for their illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine” after the US president, Donald Trump, struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from the country.

The energy and climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said on Saturday Australia did not “need or want Russian fuel” while updating reporters on the country’s fuel reserves.

But One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said it was “important to work with countries, if we can have the resources we need”, not ruling out supporting Australia making such a deal of its own.

Trump wrote on social media on Saturday morning Australian time that after a “highly successful discussion” with Putin, Russia had agreed to immediately supply “300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel” to US and global markets, which would be followed by 500,000 tons in November rising later to 3m tons, depending on “the condition of [Russia’s] diesel refineries”.

The deal was criticised by Democrats and some Republicans. Trump is under political pressure due to high diesel prices in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the deal “plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world”.

During a regular Saturday morning press conference to update Australians on the country’s fuel reserves, Bowen, who will lead negotiations at next month’s UN climate talks in Turkey, said: “We don’t need or want Russian fuel in Australia.”

“We have the arrangements in place as best as we possibly can with our trading partners to ensure that Russian fuel doesn’t flow to Australia.

“We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in the Middle East. What the United States does is a matter for them. But we won’t be changing our approach.

“We’ll continue to have the very, very firm view that Russia should not be rewarded for their illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine by any arrangements put in place as a result of the Middle East crisis … policies for other countries are a matter for them.”

Hanson, asked whether she would support Australia taking similar action to Trump, said she wanted to see more oil supply.

“If it’s going to get supplied all throughout the world, because a lot of countries are suffering from this lack of oil, I think it’s important to work with countries, if we can have the resources that we need,” she said at a press conference on the sidelines of the CPAC convention in Brisbane.

“We cannot see countries come to an absolute standstill, businesses shutting down, the cost to the consumer … I think it’s important that all countries must consider that it’s about delivering oil.”

Hanson did not answer a follow-up question about whether that should specifically include Russian oil. During her speech to CPAC, the One Nation leader called for Australia to “produce our own fuel as the world becomes more dangerous”.

Uncertainties remain in the Middle East as a result of Trump’s protracted war with Iran. He this week promised he would not launch more attacks on Iran before the midterm elections.

Bowen said the “situation internationally remains difficult” but Australia had 43 days’ worth of petrol and 31 days’ worth of diesel, which was consistent with recent updates.

“We have 51 ships on the way to Australia with fuel, and we have 3.2bn litres of the various types of fuel locked in and contracted to be delivered over the next four weeks.”

Bowen said he had met with senior Saudi Arabian representatives during a meeting in Fiji to prepare for the UN climate talks in Turkey.

“Obviously we continue to see attacks in Saudi Arabia,” he said. “But I do have confidence that the Saudi Arabian government is taking steps to ensure that the fuel is flowing as well as it possibly can be.

“We’ll continue the same approach that we’ve had all through this crisis, working closely with trading partners in south-east Asia and beyond, including India and Saudi Arabia, working very closely with our domestic refiners to ensure that they are working at full pelt.

“And I continue to be in very regular contact with the chief executives of Australia’s domestic refiners.”

australia.title: ‘Smarmy management consultant’: Angus Taylor criticised by Pauline Hanson and heckled at CPAC event
australia.snippet: Liberal leader says Coalition ‘got some things wrong’ in signing up to net zero and increasing immigration Get our new political email , ...
australia.content:
Pauline Hanson has labelled Angus Taylor a “smarmy management consultant” and told attendees of a major conservative conference that they should not trust the Coalition, as the Liberal leader came under fire from hecklers in the crowd.

But Hanson has reiterated her offer to work together with the Coalition to defeat the Labor government, suggesting attendees of the annual Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) Australia in Brisbane put the Liberals or Nationals second on their ballot papers, behind One Nation.

Hanson’s insults aimed at the Coalition came moments after Taylor had given a mea culpa to the conference, criticising past Liberal governments – in which he was a key minister – for signing up to a net zero climate target, increasing immigration, and public spending during the pandemic.

“Your frustrations about where we let you down in the recent past are understandable and reasonable. Believe me, I share those frustrations,” the opposition leader said.

CPAC Australia heard from Taylor, Hanson and Nationals leader Matt Canavan on its opening morning on Saturday. It is the first time a sitting Liberal leader has addressed the event, and comes amid One Nation consistently outpolling the Coalition.

Hanson was the best received of all three conservative leaders, receiving a standing ovation from most of the crowd as she took the stage and an even more raucous applause as she finished. Taylor’s speech received a standing ovation from less than half the crowd.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

While Taylor took a more conciliatory tone toward One Nation in his speech, Hanson’s address repeatedly slammed what she called the “uniparty”, referring to Labor and the Coalition.

“Australians despise [prime minister Anthony] Albanese … and quite frankly, they don’t want some smarmy management consultant taking his place either,” Hanson said.

Taylor, according to his own website, worked as a management consultant before entering politics, including at global consulting firm McKinsey.

Hanson told CPAC: “The uniparty have taken turns running this country into the ground. Both must be held accountable for the position they’ve put us in.”

She went on to point out the former Coalition government had made a commitment to net zero – a pledge since abolished by Taylor – and instituted the eSafety commissioner, both of which elicited boos from the audience.

“They [Liberals] signed us up to [net zero], so why would we trust them to get us out of it?” she said.

Hanson also said One Nation wanted a royal commission into net zero, including into “every decision the uniparty has made”.

But despite repeated criticism of the Coalition, Hanson said she was still keen for the conservative parties to cooperate.

“I know there are people in this room who support the Liberals and Nationals. I won’t walk away from what One Nation believes, but I will make you one comment. One Nation will work with the Liberals and Nationals to remove this Labor government,” Hanson said.

Taylor, speaking directly before Hanson, began his speech by admitting Coalition governments “got some important things wrong”. Taylor – who served in the Turnbull and Morrison ministries, including as energy minister – said they had “made the mistake of signing up to net zero”, and allowed “immigration numbers to creep up”.

He urged conference attendees to stick by the Coalition, claiming the Liberals and Nationals were “the most credible alternative government”. Taylor did not directly mention One Nation, but conceded “some of you may have doubts” about the Coalition.

“The Coalition is once again conviction-led and unashamedly on the right,” he said.

Taylor lauded the Coalition’s newly announced immigration policy, but received a small smattering of boos from the crowd when he mentioned his net overseas migration target of 130,000 then 160,000 in years three and four of his plan.

There were louder boos in a subsequent on-stage interview conducted by podcaster Karl Stefanovic, who asked several questions about how the Coalition could work together with One Nation.

Asked by Stefanovic if the conservative parties were “splitting the vote”, Taylor responded “I’m splitting nothing”, which elicited loud heckling from sections of the crowd. Several people yelled: “Answer the question”.

Taylor said he acknowledged “differences in view” among CPAC attendees, but said they were “united” in seeking political change.

Stefanovic stated: “You’re also fighting for your party’s survival”. Taylor replied: “Sure”, going on to claim the Coalition had previously been “frightened of our shadow”.

Stefanovic later interviewed Hanson and Canavan, with the One Nation leader taking the seat just vacated by Taylor.

CPAC continues over Saturday and Sunday. Other conservative speakers include the One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, the former British prime minister Liz Truss, and shadow ministers Dan Tehan and Sarah Henderson.

australia.title: Flydubai co-pilot began radicalisation in Australia, UAE prosecutors say
australia.snippet: Hammam al-Hammami’s shift towards extremism began while he was a student in Melbourne, according to Emirati attorney general Get our brea...
australia.content:
The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a flydubai jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week had been radicalised while studying in Australia, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.

Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop 29-year-old Omani national Hammam al-Hammami’s alleged attempt to hijack the plane on its way to Israel.

Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney general of the UAE, said al-Hammami’s shift towards extremism and terrorism began while he was studying at RMIT University in Melbourne.

During his time in Melbourne, he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, the attorney general said.

The statement was shared on UAE government social media and first reported by the state-run Emirati news agency, known as WAM.

According to the statement, al-Hammami allegedly told prosecutors he adopted ideas advocating violence and terrorism and drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001.

“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking,” the statement said.

Al-Hammami allegedly prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the alleged terror plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach.

Last weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017.

On Monday, RMIT University confirmed that he had studied at its Melbourne campus, but “did not successfully complete an engineering qualification”.

Contacted by Guardian Australia on Saturday, RMIT said it did not have any further comment to make while an investigation led by the Victorian joint counter-terrorism team was ongoing.

australia.title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight-loss drugs, Australian advocates say
australia.snippet: With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label Get our breaking ne...
australia.content:
Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say.

The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.

Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain and hair thinning.

The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.

While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.

Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a University of New South Wales study found in July.

Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.

“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.

Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.

Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.

“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.

“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”

Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.

“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.

GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.

Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.

The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.

The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.

The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.

They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.

“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.

“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”

QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.

“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.

australia.title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention...
australia.content:
A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.

On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”

Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.

A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

The fires occurred despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.

The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.

“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.

A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:

“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”

An Australian Border Force spokesperson said it continually reviewed safety and security arrangements across the detention network.

“Any regulatory notices issued by Comcare are assessed and responded to through established workplace health and safety processes,” the spokesperson said.

“The welfare, safety and dignity of people in immigration detention, as well as the safety of staff, remain the Department’s highest priorities.”

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

world.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
world.snippet: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the f...
world.content:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

world.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
world.snippet: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian journalists...
world.content:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

world.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
world.snippet: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme A survey of the world’s ...
world.content:
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”
